name: Panare
confidence_why: Payne & Payne 2013 (the reference grammar) put primary stress most often on the final syllable, with a few stems lexically stressed on the penult and a grammatical leftward shift before a preceding object, Gildea 1989 independently gives the same word-final default for unmarked stems and Derbyshire 1999 also has Panare stress "normally on the final" syllable; the only dissent is Meira 2006's one-line encyclopedia remark that Panare stress is usually penultimate, and Cauty 1978, who allowed stress on any syllable but said his corpus could not settle the question.

catalog_quote: [Payne & Payne 2013, Google Books snippets, feed tokenisation] ... Primary Stress and Orthographic Marking Primary stress in Panare is phonetically associated with raised pitch and increased intensity . It most often occurs on the final syllable of a word . Word- final primary stress is most evident when a word occurs in the peak of an intonation contour and ... stress marking rule: Stress is not written when it occurs on the last syllable of a word unless there is another stressed syllable in the same word . Stress (whether lexical or grammatical) is marked when it occurs anywhere other than the last syllable of a word . ... words contain final primary stress: (2) kïrïnïpến ' dog ' yutën ' goes ' yamayáj ' X knocked him / her / it down ' yamañé ' X knocks / will knock him / her / it down ' A few stems in Panare have lexically - marked stress on the penultimate syllable . However, we have encountered no minimal pairs that differ only in placement of lexical stress: (3) yompíku ' scold ' yuwarupúta ' initiate with loincloth ' eeñakató ... Secondary Stress Any heavy (typically closed) syllable carries at least secondary stress (indi- cated below by the grave accent) ... [Gildea 1989 p. 12] The accent in unmarked stems falls on the last syllable of the word, in this case the past tense suffix -ya'. [Cauty 1978 p. 2] In general, every word has one stressed syllable; the stress may be on any syllable of the word.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: The two stresses of intensity noted in the Panare language, strong and weak, will be indicated as follows: strong stress ['] weak stress : unmarked. In general, every word has one stressed syllable; the stress may be on any syllable of the word. A compound word may have more than one strong stress: for instance, "sugar mill" [karanápí/to] = |karaná pi/ to| ... has two strong stresses. The corpus does not contain any minimal pairs of contrasting stresses and does not enable us to study closely the question of the stress in the Panare language. There is still some doubt as to whether there exists a pertinent melodic stress.
new_statements.citation: Cauty, André. 1978. An approach to the phonological and syllabic systems of the Panare language (Venezuela). Amerindia 3: 85-103. Paris: Association d'Ethnolinguistique Amérindienne.
new_statements.locator: Part I 'The phonological system', sec. 1 'The stresses' (first page of Part I; p. 2 of the Amerindia re-typeset file; print pp. 85-103, i.e. c. p. 85-86); vowel-length remark in sec. I.2.2
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. (text; extracted text of pp. 1-4). Part I 'The phonological system', sec. '1-. The stresses', p. 2, reads exactly: 'The two stresses of intensity noted in the Panare language, strong and weak, will be indicated as follows: strong stress ['] weak stress : unmarked / In general, every word has one stressed syllable; the stress may be on any syllable of the word. A compound word may have more than one strong stress: for instance, "sugar mill" [karanápí/to] = |karaná pi/ to|, where [karaná] = "sugar cane", |pí/| is the radical of the verb "to press" and |to| a morpheme of finality, has two strong stresses[fn 4]. / The corpus does not contain any minimal pairs of…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Each word carries one intensity stress whose position is not fixed — it may fall on any syllable (Cauty marks it lexically in transcriptions, e.g. [karaná], [ecérkõ], [árkõ], [amanatá:ci], [pó:nã]); no minimal stress pairs were found in a 1,400-word corpus, so contrastiveness is unproven; long vowels appear always to be stressed; a possible pitch ('melodic') accent is raised but a perception test was negative.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A 'weak' stress degree is mentioned but not located; compounds may carry two strong stresses (one per member).
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds with two strong stresses; long vowels attract stress (I.2.2: 'it seems that a long vowel is also a stressed one'); in r-vowel elision 'the elided vowel never is the accentuated one'. Author stresses the analysis is preliminary ('ébauche') and based on two speakers from Caño Amarillo.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (isolated lexical items from an elicited word corpus); sentence-level pitch differences discussed separately. NB second-hand surveys disagree: Derbyshire 1999: 28 says Panare stress is contrastive and 'normally on the final syllable'; Meira 2006: 201 groups Panare with 'simple cumulative, usually penultimate, stress'. The modern primary treatment (Payne & Payne 2013, ch. 2) could not be opened and should supersede Cauty.
new_statements.identity_note: Cauty 1978 describes the speech of Caño Amarillo (southern Caicara del Orinoco area, Estado Bolívar), two speakers, data 1973-74 — Panare proper (enap1235); no dialect split in Glottolog. Krisólogo 1988 covers El Tigre/El Mato/Perro de Agua regions.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's final-syllable rule (world-2026-09-17: final stress) as the default for unmarked stems, and refines it: some stems carry a lexical accent that overrides the default (petyúma), and a syntactic accent shift moves the verb's primary stress leftward when an object NP precedes the verb. Partly reconciles Cauty 1978's 'the stress may be on any syllable of the word' (existing statement, lexical (unpredictable)): Gildea also recognises lexically accented stems but gives an explicit final-syllable default, which Cauty does not.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No phonology section; the thesis is a syntax description and the author states he has not done a thorough phonological analysis. Incidentally to the agreement-prefix discussion it states that in unmarked (lexically unaccented) stems the accent falls on the last syllable of the word (e.g. the past-tense suffix -ya' in nikitiya'), whereas a lexically accented stem such as petyúma 'hit' keeps its stem accent (nipetyúmaya'). A syntactic rule shifts the verb's primary stress leftward when the object NP immediately precedes the verb (arakon pétyumaya' 'he hit the monkey'), glossed PO 'Preceding Object'.
new_statements.exceptions: (a) lexically accented stems (petyúma) do not take word-final accent; (b) a preverbal object triggers a leftward accent shift on the verb (pétyumaya'), which disappears when the preverbal object is removed (endnote, p. 69: 'the verb will no longer take the accent for Preceding Object'). pp. 13-60 (thesis body pp. the TOC lists no phonology section.
new_statements.identity_note: Gildea 1989 is first-hand fieldwork (Caicara del Orinoco, Venezuela, 1988) on Panare (E'ñapa); no dialect is named. The author uses an early Payne & Payne phonemic system and says explicitly that he has not done a thorough phonological analysis.

readall_conflicts: Cauty 1978 (existing statement) says every word has one stressed syllable which 'may be on any syllable of the word' (lexical, unpredictable), while Gildea 1989 states a word-final default for unmarked stems with lexically accented stems as exceptions plus a syntactic leftward shift; these are compatible if Cauty's 'any syllable' reflects the lexically accented stems and the PO shift, but Cauty gives no default. Second-hand summaries already held by the project disagree with each other: Derbyshire 1999 p. 28 has stress 'normally on the final.. syllable' and 'contrastive only in PA[nare]', and the Payne & Payne 2013 Google Books snippet (ch. 2) says primary stress 'most often occurs on the final syllable of a word' with secondary stress on heavy syllables, whereas Meira 2006 (ELL2 p. 201) lists Panare among languages with 'usually penultimate' stress. Gildea 1989 sides with the final-syllable default (catalog, Derbyshire, Payne & Payne) against Meira's penultimate.
